title: India-US Trade Talks Stall as 10% Tariff Nears Expiry and Section 301 Duties Loom
excerpt: With the temporary global tariff set to lapse this month and new Section 301 investigations targeting India, New Delhi is holding out for better terms rather than accepting a rushed deal.
body:
• The temporary 10% U.S. tariff on Indian goods, imposed under Section 122 after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's IEEPA tariffs, is set to expire later this month after its 150-day authorization window.
  • India has rejected a quick trade deal with Washington, holding out for a competitive advantage over China and a guarantee against future tariff escalation.
  • The U.S. has already hit Brazil with 25% Section 301 tariffs and is expected to target India next through probes into excess industrial capacity and forced labour.
  • India's strengthened economic position — rising exports, a UK free trade deal, and eased oil prices — has given New Delhi leverage to wait rather than accept unfavorable terms.

India faces a pivotal moment in its trade relationship with the United States as the temporary 10% global tariff imposed by the Trump administration nears its expiration date this month, with no bilateral trade agreement in place and new, potentially steeper tariffs looming through Section 301 investigations.

The 10% levy, imposed under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, was the administration's fallback after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's sweeping reciprocal tariffs in February, ruling that the use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose trade duties exceeded presidential authority. Section 122 permits a temporary import surcharge of up to 15% for 150 days to address balance-of-payments concerns — a clock that is now running out.

India Holds Its Ground

Despite the approaching deadline, India has declined to rush into a deal. Recent talks between U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Indian officials in New Delhi last month ended without consensus, according to Reuters.

The breakdown centered on two key Indian demands: a tariff advantage over competitors like China, and assurance that the U.S. would not impose additional levies after the deal was signed. Washington did not provide either guarantee, an Indian government official told Reuters.

"Our position is clear — we don't intend to rush into a deal that is not on favourable terms or compromise on red lines like ceding ground on agriculture."

— Indian government official involved in trade talks, speaking to Reuters

Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said both sides remain "fully engaged" but that the deal "would not be implemented unless an advantage is ensured." Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal echoed that the framework agreement is "ready" but will be signed only "whenever it is the right time."

![President Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg) > **"The tariffs take effect July 22, two days before the 10% global tariff is scheduled to expire.

India is expected to be among the next targets."**

A U.S. official acknowledged that India had at times been "slow, bureaucratic and difficult" in the negotiations, signalling that a quick resolution is unlikely.

Section 301: The Next Wave of Tariffs

The more immediate concern for Indian exporters is a new generation of tariffs coming through Section 301 of the Trade Act, which requires country-specific investigations into unfair trade practices rather than blanket emergency powers.

On July 16, the USTR announced 25% tariffs on a broad range of Brazilian imports — furniture, ethanol, machinery, footwear, and sugar — marking the first country targeted under this new strategy. The tariffs take effect July 22, two days before the 10% global tariff is scheduled to expire.

India is expected to be among the next targets. The USTR has launched two separate Section 301 investigations affecting India: one examining allegations of excess industrial capacity across 60 economies, and another proposing tariffs of up to 12.5% on 54 countries — including India — over claims they failed to curb trade in goods produced with forced labour.

India has formally asked the USTR to reconsider the forced labour tariff proposal, arguing that the agency failed to identify any specific Indian act or policy that would constitute an "unreasonable" practice under Section 301.

Why India Can Afford to Wait

Several factors have bolstered New Delhi's bargaining position. India's goods exports rose approximately 15% year-over-year in April-June 2026, with U.S.-bound shipments remaining steady. Exports to Gulf countries have recovered to pre-war levels after disruptions from the Iran conflict.

![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

India is also diversifying its trade partnerships. A free trade agreement with the UK is set to take effect this month, and an EU deal is expected by early next year. Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India to 6.8%, and the interim U.S.-Iran peace deal has eased oil prices and improved India's current account outlook.

"Indian negotiators have gained some leverage in the talks, given its strong economy, diversification initiatives with other partners, and its strategic standing in the world," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute and a former U.S. trade official.

The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian Americans and the broader diaspora, the tariff uncertainty has direct implications. Indian IT services, pharmaceuticals, and manufactured goods exported to the U.S. could face price adjustments depending on the final tariff regime. Indian American entrepreneurs with supply chains spanning both countries face planning challenges as the trade framework remains unresolved.

The USTR's Brazil tariff announcement also raised eyebrows for India. Greer cited Brazil's preferential tariff arrangements with India and Mexico as evidence of unfair trade practices — a finding that could complicate India's trade relationships with other developing economies.

What to Watch

The immediate timeline is compressed. The 10% Section 122 tariff expires later this month. The Section 301 tariffs on Brazil take effect July 22. Industry sources told The Hindu Business Line that India is adopting a "wait-and-watch" approach, noting that the temporary tariffs could drop to zero if no new authority replaces them.

But trade analysts caution against optimism. "India realises that delaying — or even abandoning — a rushed deal may be more prudent than locking into obligations whose costs could far exceed any temporary tariff relief," said Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative and a former Indian trade negotiator.

The coming weeks will determine whether India and the U.S. can bridge their differences before the next wave of tariffs arrives — or whether the bilateral trade relationship enters a more adversarial phase.
